raw_response:
I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou pattern of `winter wheat + summer maize` on the same fields. I know this system, it matches our climate, and it is the safest way for me to keep grain output steady without making the work too complicated. In Quzhou, most rain comes in summer, so maize fits the rainy season well, while wheat gives me a stable winter-spring crop if I irrigate on time. At my age, I would not gamble on a more complicated rotation or a specialty cash crop that needs closer market timing and more delicate management.

I will use improved winter wheat seed and hybrid summer maize seed. For wheat, I will prepare the land with rotary tillage after maize harvest, sow in mid-October, put most phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, split nitrogen between base and topdressing, irrigate at the key stages, and keep pesticide use limited to what is needed for common weeds, aphids, rust, and mildew. After wheat harvest in June, I will direct-seed summer maize with no-tillage into the wheat stubble to save time and moisture. For maize, I will rely mainly on rainfall, add one irrigation only if the soil is too dry, apply nitrogen in split doses, and control weeds and corn borers with a small number of sprays. I will return straw to the field where possible and aim for steady yield rather than the highest possible yield, because that is the more practical choice for me.
